scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

What a lovely tradition! Serving tea to elders in the family is a thoughtful and respectful gesture, especially in many Asian cultures. However, I can understand why it might take a significant amount of time, especially if there are many elders to be served. If I had to suggest a compromise, I would recommend shortening the ceremony while still maintaining its essence. Here are a few ideas: 1. **Simplify the tea-serving process**: Instead of serving each elder individually, consider having a designated server or two who can serve tea to multiple elders at the same time. This can help speed up the process without losing the personal touch. 2. **Limit the number of elders served**: If there are many elders in the family, consider limiting the number of people who are served tea. This could be based on age, family relationship, or other criteria. 3. **Combine the tea-serving ceremony with other activities**: Consider combining the tea-serving ceremony with other pre-banquet activities, such as a family photo shoot or a brief welcome speech. This can help make the most of the time and create a more dynamic atmosphere. 4. **Make it a more symbolic gesture**: If the tea-serving ceremony is more about showing respect and gratitude to the elders, consider making it a more symbolic gesture. For example, the couple could serve tea to a select few elders, and then have a more general toast or welcome to the rest of the family. Ultimately, the decision to keep or shorten the tea-serving ceremony depends on the couple's priorities and the preferences of their family members. If the ceremony is an important part of the family's tradition and culture, it's worth preserving.
